name: Katsakáti
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Michael, Lev David; Beier, Christine; Escamilla, Ramón; Piqueras-Brunet, Marta. 2009. Katsakáti: El idioma antiguo del pueblo de Andoas. Andoas Viejo / San Lorenzo, Loreto, Perú: Proyecto de Documentación del Idioma Andoa (Katsakáti), University of California, Berkeley & Cabeceras Aid Project. 27 pp. Open PDF:http://www.cabeceras.org/anb_katsakati_jun2009.pdf(saved; scanned print version)
catalog_locator: Parte 1, §1.3 'El tono de la voz', pp. 9-10; accent-marked lexicon in Parte 3 and Parte 5, pp. 18-27 ff.
catalog_quote: Cada palabra del idioma katsakáti tiene una parte que pronunciamos con un tono de voz más alto que las demás partes. Señalamos con una tilde la vocal que se pronuncia con el tono alto: ocháte ¡vamos ya! En el caso de las vocales largas, generalmente acentuámos la primera letra de la vocal larga (recuerda que escribimos dos letras pero pronunciamos sólo una, más larga): wéeno sachavaca, kíinti picaflor. En general, cada palabra tiene un solo tono alto, pero algunas palabras muy largas tienen más de uno. Si los dos tonos son igualmente altos, usamos la misma tilde para los dos. En cambio, si un tono es ligeramente más bajo que el otro, usamos una tilde diferente (`) para ese tono (no tan alto) y una normal (´) para el tono más alto: ijátyawkwáro zúngaro blanco, kwajàkeró boa.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Every word of the Katsakáti language has one part that we pronounce with a higher pitch than the other parts. We mark with an accent the vowel that is pronounced with the high pitch: ocháte 'let's go now!'. In the case of long vowels we generally put the accent on the first letter of the long vowel [...]: wéeno 'tapir', kíinti 'hummingbird'. In general each word has a single high pitch, but some very long words have more than one. If the two pitches are equally high we use the same accent mark for both. If instead one pitch is slightly lower than the other, we use a different mark ( ` ) for that (less high) pitch and a normal one ( ´ ) for the highest pitch: [...] kwajàkeró 'boa'.

En general, cada palabra tiene un solo tono alto, pero algunas palabras muy largas tienen más de…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level culminative prominence realized as high pitch: each word has one syllable (vowel) pronounced on a higher pitch than the rest, marked with an acute accent on every recorded form; the source states no rule predicting which syllable carries it, and the marked position varies across the booklet's ~180 forms (e.g. amáka 'stick', kakarája 'hen', tsíma 'maiden', náakero 'caiman' vs. anapachá 'sky', newá 'tinamou', iyá 'earth', awashakó 'fingernail'; by my tally roughly final > penult > antepenult), so placement appears lexically specified (my inference, not the authors' claim). Peeke 1954 marks accents on the same lexemes in the same places where they overlap (amáka, iyá).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Some very long words carry two high pitches; if equal both get ´, if one is slightly lower it is written with a grave ` (e.g. ijátyawkwáro 'white zúngaro catfish', kwajàkeró 'boa', kwàpajáno) — i.e. a primary vs. weaker secondary prominence is recognized, position not rule-governed in the text.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; long vowels take the mark on their first letter ('generalmente'); the vowel o varies freely with u (segmental, not prosodic).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word in citation form ('cada palabra'), elicited in 2009 from the last two rememberers (Juan Mucushua, María Sandi) at Andoas Viejo, río Pastaza, Loreto — a remembered lexicon of isolated words and short phrases, not connected speech. The authors describe the prominence in pitch terms ('tono de voz más alto') in a community primer; they do not use the words 'acento'/'stress' analytically nor claim (un)predictability. SAPhon (same research group) codes Andoa 'tone: False'. Peeke 1954 independently called Shimigae 'de alta tonalidad.. tal vez un ritmo complicado' and deferred phonetic analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted/checked primary sources describe the Zaparoan language of Andoas on the río Pastaza, Loreto, Peru = Glottolog ando1255 [anb]: Peeke 1954 under the names Shimigae/Andoa (fluent elderly speakers, 1951-53), Michael et al. 2009 under the autonym Katsakáti (last rememberers Juan Mucushua and María Sandi, Andoas Viejo, 2009; last speaker Hipólito Arahuanaza d. 2012). Peeke notes the townspeople said the 'true Andoa' of their fathers resembled Murato/Candoshi, so 'Andoa' as an ethnonym is ambiguous, but the language described in both works is the Zaparoan Shimigae/Katsakáti. The 2009 booklet's Cuadro 1 also cites Arabela, Iquito and Záparo forms (not Andoa) — excluded from the reading. The Ecuadorian 'Andoa/Andwa' revitalization community (Pastaza, Ecuador) uses Peeke's materials for the same language.

sources.citation: Peeke, Catherine. 1954. Shimigae, idioma que se extingue. Perú Indígena 5(13): 171-178; repr. 1959 in Estudios acerca de las lenguas huarani (auca), shimigae y zápara (Quito: Ministerio de Educación / ILV), pp. 18-28; reprinted 2023 with an introduction by Jorge Gómez Rendón in Antropología Cuadernos de Investigación (PUCE, Quito) 28: 91-97. DOI 10.26807/raci.vi28.323
sources.note: Explicitly defers phonetics ('la discusión de estos asuntos fonéticos no atañen al presente trabajo'); only an impression that Shimigae sounds 'nasal y de alta tonalidad; que tiene tal vez un ritmo complicado' (p. 94 of reprint). Example words carry acute accents (amáka, áni, nárjara, kómai, numátu, apíjiya, iyá, peyáno') without any statement of what they mark or where accent falls. Notes phrase-final glottal stop as an utterance-level feature (§III.D).
